config.title: :has()

intro.title: :has()
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a simple interactive webpage that uses the CSS `:has()` pseudo-class to style elements based on their contents. You will learn how `:has()` allows you to select and style a parent element when it contains specific child elements, enabling more dynamic and conditional styling without JavaScript. The main technologies involved are pure CSS, focusing on selectors and pseudo-classes. By the end, you will understand the syntax and practical applications of `:has()` to create responsive and context-aware designs.
intro.usecase: The :has() selector is commonly used in modern web applications to create dynamic, context-aware interfaces. For instance, in a dashboard with collapsible panels, you can use :has() to style a panel's header differently when its content section is expanded. In complex forms, you can highlight a fieldset when any of its required inputs are invalid. E-commerce sites often use :has() to apply special styling to product cards that contain a 'sale' badge or out-of-stock label. This allows developers to write cleaner CSS that responds to the actual state of the DOM without adding extra JavaScript classes.

objectives: Apply the :has() pseudo-class to style a parent element based on the presence of a child element.
Construct a CSS rule using :has() to conditionally format a list when it contains a specific list item.
Manipulate the visual state of a form container when an input within it is focused.
Configure a navigation menu to highlight a section only if it contains an active link.
Implement a card layout that changes its border when an image inside it has a caption.
Update a grid container's spacing when any of its items have a particular class.
Integrate :has() with other pseudo-classes like :hover to create interactive component states.

steps.title: Create basic HTML structure for :has() demonstration
steps.instruction: Create a simple HTML structure with nested elements to demonstrate the :has() selector functionality. Add a div with class 'container' containing a heading, a paragraph, and a nested div with a button inside.
steps.hint: Start with a div element that has a class of 'container'. Inside it, add an h1 heading, a p paragraph, and another div. Inside that nested div, add a button element.
steps.expectedOutcome: You will have a basic HTML structure with nested elements that we can later style using the :has() selector.
successCriteria: The code contains a div with class 'container' that includes an h1 heading, a p paragraph, and a nested div with a button inside.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your structure includes all required elements: a div with class 'container' containing an h1, a p, and a nested div with a button.
steps.feedbackWrong: Create a div with class 'container' that contains an h1 heading, a paragraph, and another div with a button inside it.

steps.title: Add CSS file and link it to HTML
steps.instruction: Create a CSS file named 'styles.css' and link it to your HTML document by adding a <link> tag inside the <head> section.
steps.hint: Use <link rel='stylesheet' href='styles.css'> in the <head> of your HTML.
steps.analogousExample:
/* Linking a CSS file */
<head>
  <link rel="stylesheet" href="styles.css">
</head>

steps.instruction: In your CSS file, add a style rule to set the font size of all paragraphs to 18px.
steps.hint: Use the element selector 'p' followed by curly braces and the property 'font-size'.
steps.expectedOutcome: All paragraph text in the HTML will appear larger at 18px.
successCriteria: A CSS rule using the 'p' selector with 'font-size: 18px;' is present.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're using the correct selector and property.
steps.feedbackWrong: Check that you're targeting paragraphs with 'p' and setting 'font-size' to 18px.

steps.instruction: Add a CSS rule that uses the :has() selector to style the parent container when it contains a specific child element.

steps.title: Combine :has() with other pseudo-classes
steps.instruction: Create a selector that styles a parent element only when it contains a child element that is currently being hovered over. Use the :has() selector combined with the :hover pseudo-class.
steps.hint: Think about selecting a parent element based on the hover state of its child. The syntax will look like 'parent:has(child:hover) { ... }'.
steps.expectedOutcome: A CSS selector that combines :has() with :hover to apply styles to a parent element when its child is hovered.
successCriteria: The code includes a valid CSS selector using :has() combined with :hover pseudo-class.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your selector uses both :has() and :hover together. The syntax should be 'parent:has(child:hover) { ... }'.
steps.feedbackWrong: The selector doesn't properly combine :has() with :hover. Remember that :has() can contain other pseudo-classes inside its parentheses.

steps.title: Apply :has() with attribute selectors
steps.instruction: Create a CSS rule that uses the :has() selector with an attribute selector to style elements based on whether they contain a child with a specific attribute. For example, style a div that contains an input with a 'required' attribute.
steps.hint: Combine :has() with an attribute selector inside it, like div:has(input[required]) { ... }
steps.expectedOutcome: A new CSS rule that uses :has() with an attribute selector to target elements based on child attributes.
successCriteria: The code includes a valid CSS rule using :has() combined with an attribute selector (e.g., [required], [disabled], [type]).
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your selector uses :has() with an attribute selector inside it (e.g., element:has(child[attribute])).
steps.feedbackWrong: That doesn't match the requirement. Create a CSS rule that uses :has() with an attribute selector to style elements based on child attributes.

steps.hint: Use the :has() selector with multiple conditions separated by commas inside the parentheses.
steps.expectedOutcome: The selector will apply styles to parent elements that contain both specified child elements.
successCriteria: A :has() selector is written that checks for both a <strong> element and an element with class 'highlight'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure your selector checks for both a <strong> element AND an element with class 'highlight'.
steps.feedbackWrong: Try again. The selector should use :has() to check for two different child elements.

steps.title: Use :has() for form validation styling
steps.instruction: Create a CSS selector that uses :has() to style a form container when it contains an invalid input element.
steps.hint: Use the :has() pseudo-class with the :invalid pseudo-class inside to target a form that has an invalid input.
steps.expectedOutcome: A CSS rule that uses :has() with :invalid to apply styling to a form container based on invalid input presence.
successCriteria: The CSS selector uses :has() with :invalid to target a form container that contains an invalid input element.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your selector uses :has() with :invalid to target a form container that contains an invalid input element.
steps.feedbackWrong: The selector doesn't correctly use :has() for form validation. Try creating a selector that styles a form container when it has an invalid input element inside.
